sessions.title: CPU

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: ● Beginner: What is a CPU core vs a thread?
● Senior: How does context switching impact performance, and how would you diagnose excessive context switching on a production server?
● Architect: How do you approach CPU capacity planning across a virtualized enterprise fleet, considering licensing costs, vCPU oversubscription ratios, and workload types?
anchors: Think of the CPU as a chef in a kitchen: cache is the ingredients on the counter (fast to grab), RAM is the pantry (slower, has to walk there), storage is the grocery store (much slower still). Cores are multiple chefs working in parallel; hyper-threading is one chef juggling two dishes efficiently but not truly cooking two at once.
sessions.summary: What a CPU actually is: cores, threads, clock speed, cache, and why 'GHz' is not a performance score.

sessions.title: Memory

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: ● Beginner: What's the difference between RAM and storage?
● Architect: How would you design memory allocation and overcommit policy across a virtualization cluster hosting mixed workloads (databases vs stateless web servers)?
anchors: If storage is the grocery store and cache is the counter ingredients (from Session 1's analogy), RAM is the refrigerator and pantry in your kitchen — much faster to access than the store, holds a meaningful amount, but everything spoils/empties if the power (electricity) goes out. You keep only what you're actively cooking with today, not your entire life's food supply.
sessions.summary: RAM: modules, channels, ECC vs non-ECC, speeds, and how virtual memory swaps to disk.

sessions.title: Storage

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: ● Beginner: What's the difference between an HDD and an SSD?
● Architect: How would you design tiered storage for an enterprise with databases, file servers, and long- term archival needs, balancing cost and performance?
anchors: Continuing the kitchen analogy: if cache is counter ingredients, RAM is the fridge/pantry, then storage is the actual warehouse/cellar — everything you own long-term, accessible but a real walk away, and it's still there whether the power is on or off. You wouldn't cook directly from the warehouse every time (too slow), but everything ultimately originates from and returns to it.
sessions.summary: Disks and storage tiers: HDD vs SSD vs NVMe, SMART health, RAID levels, and partitioning.

sessions.title: Motherboard

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: ● Beginner: What is the role of the motherboard in a computer system?
● Intermediate: What is a chipset, and what does it control?
● Architect: When specifying a new server platform for a database cluster, which motherboard-level specs (PCIe lanes, RAM slots/ceiling, socket count) would you scrutinize, and why?
anchors: The motherboard is the kitchen itself in our ongoing kitchen analogy — the counters, the plumbing, the electrical wiring that lets the fridge (RAM), pantry (storage), and chef (CPU) actually work together in the same space. You can have the best chef and best ingredients, but without a functioning kitchen connecting them, nothing gets cooked.
sessions.summary: The motherboard: chipset, buses, slots, POST codes, and what each diagnostic beep means.

sessions.title: Power

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: ● Beginner: What does a power supply unit (PSU) actually do?
● Intermediate: Why do enterprise servers typically have two power supplies, and what could defeat that redundancy?
● Architect: How would you design power redundancy (feeds, PDUs, UPS, generator) for a new data center build to eliminate single points of failure?
anchors: Power is the electricity flowing into the kitchen itself — without it, the fridge (RAM), the stove (CPU), and the pantry lighting (storage access) simply don't function, no matter how well-designed the kitchen (motherboard) is. A UPS is like a generator-powered flashlight you grab the instant the lights flicker — enough to finish plating the current dish safely, not to cook a full dinner.
sessions.summary: Power supplies and power delivery: wattage, efficiency, transient spikes, and UPS sizing.

sessions.title: Firmware

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: ● Beginner: What is the difference between BIOS and UEFI?
● Intermediate: What is Secure Boot, and what threat does it specifically defend against?
● Senior: A server fails to detect a bootable USB installer — what firmware-level factors would you check?
● Architect: How would you design a firmware security baseline (Secure Boot, TPM, password policy, update cadence) to apply consistently across a mixed-vendor server fleet?
anchors: If the motherboard (Session 4) is the kitchen and power (Session 5) is the electricity, firmware is the kitchen's very first automatic safety check the moment the lights come on — verifying the stove ignites, the fridge compressor runs, the outlets are live — before the chef (the OS) is even allowed to walk in and start cooking.
sessions.summary: Firmware: BIOS vs UEFI, Secure Boot, TPM, and flashing risk.

sessions.title: Virtualization

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: ● Beginner: What is the difference between a Type 1 and Type 2 hypervisor?
● Senior: Multiple VMs on a host are experiencing performance issues simultaneously — how do you diagnose whether it's a host-level resource contention issue?

● Architect: How would you design a virtualization cluster's resource allocation policy (CPU/memory overcommit ratios, storage tiering) for a mixed workload of databases, web servers, and domain controllers?
anchors: If Sessions 1-6 built one fully functioning kitchen, virtualization is building walls to divide that single kitchen into several independent kitchens, each with its own stove, fridge, and pantry access — sharing the same building, plumbing, and electricity (the physical hardware), but each chef (guest OS) believes they have their own private kitchen entirely.
sessions.summary: Virtualisation concepts, hypervisors, Type 1 vs Type 2, and VM resource overhead.

sessions.title: Boot Process

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: ● Intermediate: What's the difference between a bootloader and a kernel, and why are they separate stages?
● Architect: How would you design a zero-touch, automated OS deployment pipeline (PXE, answer files/cloud-init) for provisioning dozens of new servers consistently?
anchors: Think of the boot process as a relay race: the firmware (Session 6) runs the first leg and hands the baton to the bootloader, which runs a short leg and hands off to the kernel, which runs a longer leg and hands off to the init system/services, which finally hands the baton to you at the login screen. If the race stalls, you just need to find which runner still has the baton.
sessions.summary: The full cold-boot sequence from power-on to a login prompt, and where it can break.

sessions.title: Hardware Troubleshooting

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: ● Beginner: A computer won't turn on at all — what's the first thing you check?
● Senior: You've replaced a part and the symptom returns days later — what does that suggest, and how do you proceed?
● Architect: How would you design a hardware health monitoring and alerting strategy across a large server fleet to catch failures before they cause outages?
anchors: Hardware troubleshooting is being the detective in the kitchen you've now fully built (Sessions 1-8): when a dish comes out wrong, a good detective doesn't replace the whole kitchen — they ask what changed, check the obvious things first (is the stove even on? Session 5), then narrow down systematically (was it the ingredient, the equipment, or the chef's technique?) until the actual culprit is found.
sessions.summary: A disciplined hardware troubleshooting process: identify, theorise, test, verify.

sessions.title: Windows

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is the difference between kernel mode and user mode, and why does the separation exist?
What is the role of the HAL (Hardware Abstraction Layer)?
Why can a single bad driver cause a full Blue Screen, but a crashing application usually doesn't crash the OS?
anchors: Ring 0 = trusted, Ring 3 = sandboxed. Everything an app wants from hardware must cross that line through a system call — like a bank customer (user mode) who can never touch the vault directly and must always go through a teller (kernel mode).
HAL is the universal power adapter: it lets the same 'device' (the Windows kernel) plug into different-shaped 'outlets' (chipsets) without being redesigned.
Access token = an ID badge with a list of doors it can open, issued once at login and checked by a security guard (the Security Reference Monitor) at every single door (object) along the way.
sessions.summary: Windows as an operating system: editions, features, registry, and the shell.

sessions.title: Linux

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is the difference between the Linux kernel and a Linux distribution?
What is SELinux and how is it different from standard file permissions?
Why are containers Linux-native technology?
anchors: fork() then exec() is like photocopying yourself, then having the photocopy put on a completely different person's clothes and ID — the process exists first, and only afterward becomes the new program.

DAC is the lock on your office door (you control who has a key); MAC (SELinux) is building security that still won't let you into the server room even with a valid key, because policy says so — regardless of whose door it is.

Everything is a file: Linux treats devices, processes (/proc), and even kernel settings (/sys) as if they were files you can read and write — this single idea is why so much of Linux can be automated with simple text tools.
sessions.summary: Linux as an operating system: distributions, the filesystem layout, and package managers.

sessions.title: Kernel

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is a context switch, and why is it not free?
What's the difference between a monolithic and a microkernel, and which does Linux use?
What happens, at the kernel level, when a user-mode program calls read() on a file?
Why is a kernel-level vulnerability considered more severe than a vulnerability in a user-mode application?
anchors: The kernel is the air-traffic controller: it never flies the plane (runs application logic) itself, but every plane (thread) that wants to take off, land, or change course must go through it.
A context switch is like a surgeon scrubbing out of one operation and back into another — necessary sometimes, but every switch costs real time that isn't spent operating (computing).

System calls are the embassy: user-mode code can't act directly on foreign soil (hardware), so it submits a formal request at the one recognized checkpoint, and the kernel decides whether and how to grant it.
sessions.summary: The kernel: system calls, modules, and what runs in ring 0 versus user space.

sessions.title: Processes

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is the difference between a process and a program?
How does copy-on-write make fork() efficient?
What's the difference between a process being 'blocked' and being 'hung'?
anchors: fork() is photocopying yourself mid-sentence; exec() is that photocopy immediately putting on a different uniform and starting an entirely different job.

A zombie process is an unsigned resignation letter sitting on a manager's desk — the employee (process) has already left, but HR (the kernel) can't close the file until the manager (parent) formally signs off (calls wait()).

Process isolation is apartment walls: each tenant (process) has their own locked space, and reaching into a neighbor's apartment requires going through a shared, supervised channel (IPC) — never straight through the wall.
sessions.summary: Processes: creating, inspecting, signalling and terminating them.

sessions.title: Threads

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What's the fundamental difference between a process and a thread?
What is a race condition, and how do you prevent one?
What's the difference between concurrency and parallelism?
What is a deadlock, and what are the typical conditions that cause one?
anchors: A process is a house; threads are roommates. Roommates (threads) share the same kitchen and living room (memory) — convenient, but if one leaves a mess (corrupts shared data) or starts a fire (crashes), it affects everyone in the house, not just them.
A mutex is a single bathroom key in a shared house — whoever holds it has exclusive use, and everyone else waits their turn outside the door, no matter how many roommates want in at once.

Concurrency is juggling three balls by catching and throwing them in quick succession; parallelism is three separate people each throwing one ball at the same time — juggling looks similar from a distance, but only one of these is truly simultaneous.
sessions.summary: Threads and concurrency: scheduling, contention, and why a thread can starve.

sessions.title: Memory Management

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is virtual memory, and why do operating systems use it instead of letting processes address physical RAM directly?
Explain the difference between a minor (soft) page fault and a major (hard) page fault. Which one should worry you more, and why?
A Linux server shows almost 0 MB 'free' in `free -h` but the application is running fine. Is this a problem?
What triggers the Linux OOM Killer, and how does it decide which process to kill?
What is thrashing, and what OS-level metric would you check first to confirm it's happening?
How does ASLR improve security, and what class of attack does it primarily defend against?
A Java application's container keeps getting OOM-killed even though `-Xmx` is set below the container's memory limit. What else could be consuming memory?
What is the difference between a process's 'committed' memory and its 'working set' (Windows) or 'resident set size' (Linux)?
How do huge pages improve performance, and what workloads benefit most from them?
anchors: Think of virtual memory as a hotel: every guest (process) gets their own room number (virtual address) that always looks the same to them, but the hotel (OS/MMU) can quietly change which physical room (RAM frame) that number maps to, or even move the guest's stuff to storage (swap) without the guest noticing.
Page fault = 'the OS's librarian had to actually go fetch the book' — minor fault: book was in the back room (RAM, just not on your desk); major fault: book was in the off-site archive (disk).
Copy-on-write = 'shared Google Doc in view-only mode until someone tries to edit — only then does it fork into their own copy.'
OOM Killer = 'the fire marshal at max capacity: forcibly picks and removes whoever is taking up the most space' when the building (RAM+swap) is truly full.
17. Connections — Ties to Every Prior Session
sessions.summary: Memory management: virtual memory, paging, swapping, and OOM behaviour.

sessions.title: Drivers

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is a driver, and why does it need to run in kernel mode rather than user mode for most high- performance devices?
What is DMA, and why can a buggy driver's DMA handling corrupt memory unrelated to the device it controls?
What is the top-half/bottom-half (or ISR/DPC) split in interrupt handling, and why does it exist?
What is a 'Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver' (BYOVD) attack, and what OS feature helps defend against it?
How does Linux decide which kernel module to load for a newly detected PCI device?
Why might a cloud VM fail to boot if the correct virtual hardware drivers (e.g., virtio, ENA) aren't present in the OS image?
What's the difference between installing a driver and a driver actually binding to a device — and how would you check binding status on Linux?
Why do enterprises test firmware and driver updates together rather than independently?
anchors: Think of a driver as a translator at a business meeting: the OS speaks one universal business language (generic I/O calls), the hardware speaks its own native dialect, and the driver sits between them translating both directions in real time.
Kernel-mode driver = 'employee with a master key to every door in the building' — powerful and fast, but if they make a mistake, the damage isn't contained to one room.
ISR/DPC split = 'a nurse doing rapid triage (ISR: stop the bleeding, flag it urgent) before handing off to the doctor for the actual treatment (DPC: do the real work) later.'

BYOVD attack = 'sneaking in with someone else's valid employee badge (a signed but flawed driver) instead of forging your own — security checks the badge is real, not whether the badge-holder should be trusted with that door.'
17. Connections — Ties to Every Prior Session
sessions.summary: Drivers: the kernel interface, the driver store, and why signed drivers matter.

sessions.title: Services

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is the difference between a service being 'running' and a service being 'healthy'? Why does that distinction matter operationally?
A Linux service works fine when started manually but fails at boot. What's your troubleshooting approach?
Why is it considered a security risk for a service to run as LocalSystem or root when it doesn't need to?
What is a Group Managed Service Account (gMSA) and what problem does it solve?
What happens if a service doesn't respond to a stop signal within the grace period during shutdown?
How would you detect an unauthorized/malicious service that an attacker planted for persistence?
What is the purpose of socket activation (systemd .socket units), and what problem does it solve versus starting everything at boot?
Why might monitoring tooling check a service's actual application-level health endpoint instead of just trusting the OS's 'running' status?
anchors: Think of a service manager as a building's night shift supervisor: it knows which systems (services) must be running unattended overnight, in what order to switch them on, what to do if one trips a breaker (crashes), and it keeps a logbook (Event Log/journald) of everything that happened.
'Running but not healthy' = a shop's lights are on and the door is unlocked, but the cash register is broken — open for business by outward appearance, unable to actually serve anyone.

Service dependency ordering = a restaurant kitchen: you cannot plate the dish (start the app service) before the oven has preheated (the database is ready) — skip that ordering and you get a 'started' plate that's actually raw.
Least-privilege service account = giving the night janitor a key that only opens the supply closet, not the vault — they can still do their job, but a stolen key doesn't hand over everything.
17. Connections — Ties to Every Prior Session
sessions.summary: Services and init systems, and how they differ between Windows and Linux.

sessions.title: Logging OSLevel

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is the difference between the Windows Application, System, and Security event logs?
Why is Event ID 1102 significant, and what does it tell an investigator?
Why might expected security events simply not appear in a log at all, even though nothing was cleared?
What's the difference between journald's volatile and persistent storage modes, and why does that distinction matter for incident response?
How would you detect that an attacker attempted to clear or tamper with logs on a compromised host?
Why is accurate time synchronization (NTP) critical to the usefulness of logs during a multi-server incident investigation?
What is auditd, and how does it differ in purpose from general-purpose syslog/journald logging?
Why do enterprises ship logs off-host to a centralized system rather than relying solely on local log storage?
anchors: Think of OS logging as a building's security camera system: if a camera (audit category) was never installed pointed at a particular door, no amount of investigating afterward will produce footage of who walked through it.
Event ID 1102 (Security log cleared) = the equivalent of an alarm that goes off specifically when someone tries to erase the security tapes — the act of hiding evidence becomes evidence itself.
Facility.severity in syslog = an envelope's return address (facility: which department sent it) plus its urgency stamp (severity: how important it is) — routing rules sort mail by both together.
Centralized log shipping = mailing a copy of every important document to a safety-deposit box the moment it's created, so a fire (or an intruder) in the local office can't destroy the only copy.
17. Connections — Ties to Every Prior Session
sessions.summary: Operating-system level logging: Windows event logs, syslog and journald.

sessions.title: File Systems

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is the difference between a file system's metadata and its data, and why does that distinction matter for performance and consistency?
Explain journaling and why it's necessary for crash consistency. What does a copy-on-write file system do differently?
What's happening, and how do you confirm it?
What is an inode, and why doesn't it store the file's name?
What's the difference between a hard link and a symbolic link, and what happens to each if the original file is deleted?
Why does deleting a file not necessarily make its data unrecoverable, and what does that mean for decommissioning storage hardware?
Why is object storage (like Amazon S3) not considered a true file system, and what problems can arise from treating it like one?
What happens at the file system level when a power loss occurs mid-write, and how does the system recover on next boot?
Why might an enterprise choose XFS over ext4 (or vice versa) for a specific workload?
anchors: Think of a file system as a library's card catalog plus its shelves: the catalog (metadata/inode/MFT) tells you exactly where a book lives and who's allowed to check it out, while the shelves (data blocks) hold the actual pages — losing the catalog doesn't destroy the books, but it makes them nearly impossible to find.

Journaling = a construction crew's work order posted before they start: if the crew is interrupted mid-job, the next shift reads the work order to know exactly what was in progress and finish or undo it cleanly, rather than guessing from a half-built wall.

Inode exhaustion = a parking garage that's run out of numbered parking spots even though there's technically open pavement — the constraint isn't physical room, it's the fixed count of assignable slots.

Copy-on-write = never erasing a whiteboard, only writing the new version on a fresh whiteboard and then pointing everyone to the new one — the old board still exists intact until someone deliberately wipes it (a snapshot you can always roll back to).
17. Connections — Ties to Every Prior Session
sessions.summary: File systems: NTFS, ext4, XFS and their journaling behaviour.

sessions.title: Permissions

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What do SUID and SGID do, and why are they both useful and a common security risk?
Why is it best practice to assign permissions to groups rather than individual user accounts?
A user can see a folder in Explorer/File Manager but gets denied when opening a file inside it — what permission combination would cause that?
How would you identify all SUID root binaries on a Linux server, and why would you want to?
anchors: POSIX rwx = three keyrings on one keychain: owner, group, everyone else — always in that fixed order, always only those three.
chmod numbers = read(4) + write(2) + execute(1), like a simple point system per class — 7 means you unlocked all three, 5 means you skipped write.
NTFS Deny beats Allow = a bouncer's "no" always overrules a promoter's "yes," no matter how many promoters vouched for you.
SUID = wearing someone else's badge for one task only, then handing it back the moment the task ends.
Least privilege = giving someone the one specific key they need for their job, not a master key "just in case."
sessions.summary: Permissions and ownership: ugo/rwx, ACLs, and diagnosing permission problems.

sessions.title: Users

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is a SID (or UID), and why does Windows/Linux rely on it rather than the username as the true identity of an account?
Why are service accounts a higher security risk than typical human accounts, and how would you govern them?
What's the difference between a local user account and a domain user account, and when would each be appropriate?
A user reports their account is locked out again minutes after IT unlocks it — how do you investigate the root cause?
What is account lockout policy, and what's the security tradeoff involved in setting the threshold too low versus too high?
How would you find all user accounts in an Active Directory environment that haven't logged in during the last 90 days?
anchors: User account = employee badge; it proves identity to the system but doesn't itself open any doors — permissions and groups are the doors.
UID/SID = the badge's embedded chip, not the printed name on the front — the system trusts the chip, not the name.
Disable before delete = take the badge away and deactivate it, but keep it in the drawer in case HR or legal needs to ask questions about it later.
Service account = a badge issued to a robot, not a person — it never sleeps, never quits, and needs its own separate security policy.
Account lockout = three wrong door-code attempts and the keypad locks itself for a while — a defense against someone guessing all night.
sessions.summary: Users: local accounts, password aging, and service accounts.

sessions.title: Groups

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What's the difference between Domain Local, Global, and Universal group scope in AD, and when would you use each?
A user was just added to a group but still can't access the resource — what's your troubleshooting process?
Why can nested groups be a security risk even when each individual group's permissions look reasonable?
How would you design a group structure from scratch for a support organization with agents, leads, and specialized review teams?
What is a dynamic/rule-based group, and what's the risk of a misconfigured membership rule?
How would you identify and clean up stale or empty groups in a large Active Directory environment?
anchors: Group = lanyard color; the security desk checks the lanyard, not each individual badge, and doors are configured once per color, not once per person.
A-G-DL-P = Accounts wear a Global lanyard for their role, and that lanyard gets clipped onto a Domain Local keyring that actually opens the door — Permissions live on the keyring, not the lanyard.
Nested groups = Russian nesting dolls of access — opening the outer doll doesn't tell you everything hidden inside the smaller ones without actually checking each layer.
Distribution group vs. security group = a mailing list sign-up sheet versus a building keycard — one routes messages, the other opens doors, and confusing the two is a real risk.
Stale group membership = an old lanyard nobody collected when someone changed teams — still opens doors it shouldn't, silently, until someone actually checks.
sessions.summary: Groups, memberships, and the difference between primary and supplementary groups.

sessions.title: Package Management

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is dependency hell, and how do modern package managers try to avoid or resolve it?
Why might an enterprise run its own internal package repository/mirror instead of pulling directly from the public internet?
What's the difference between an OS-level package manager (apt) and a language-level one (pip/npm), and why do both need to exist?
How would you safely apply security patches across a large server fleet without risking an unexpected outage?
What is package signing, and what specific attack does it protect against?
Why is manually deleting a package's files (instead of using the package manager to remove it) a bad practice?
anchors: Package manager = hardware store inventory system: tracked, versioned stock that won't let you take the last box of bolts three other projects still need.

Low-level vs. high-level tool = the delivery truck driver (dpkg/rpm, installs exactly what's handed to them) versus the store manager (apt/dnf, figures out everything else that needs to be ordered first).
Dependency hell = trying to fit two custom-order parts into the same slot, where satisfying one supplier's spec breaks the other's.
Package signing = a tamper-evident seal on a shipped box — if the seal's broken or missing, you don't trust what's inside, no matter how legitimate the label looks.
Version pinning = deliberately keeping one specific tool in the toolbox even after a newer model comes out, because you know exactly why the old one still fits the job.
sessions.summary: Package management: RPM and dnf, repositories, and what Flatpak changes in RHEL 10.

sessions.title: Networking Stack

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: A user says they have an IP address but can't reach anything outside their subnet. What OS-level setting would you check first, and why?
What's the difference between TCP and UDP at the OS stack level, and when would an application choose one over the other?
What is ARP, and why does a host need it even if it already knows the destination IP address?
How would you troubleshoot "this one application can't connect to the server" when other applications on the same machine connect fine?
What's the difference between a host's routing table and a router's routing table?
anchors: Postal system analogy: Socket = mailroom clerk, TCP/UDP = signed-receipt-or-not decision, IP = address on the envelope, NIC driver = delivery truck.
Bottom-up troubleshooting mnemonic: "Link, Local IP, Local Gateway, Remote IP, Name, Port" — walk the stack from the wire up to the application.
"ipconfig /all shows you the truth, ipconfig alone shows you the summary" — always use /all when actually troubleshooting.
sessions.summary: The networking stack: sockets, the port table, and which services listen by default.

sessions.title: OSIModel

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: Can you name and briefly describe all seven layers of the OSI Model, in order?
What's the difference between a packet, a frame, and a segment, and which OSI layer does each belong to?
Where does a switch operate in the OSI Model? Where does a router operate? Where does a firewall operate?
If a user can ping a server but can't load a website hosted on it, which OSI layers have you already confirmed are working, and which layer would you check next?
Why do we still teach a 7-layer model when most real-world networks are actually built on the 4-layer TCP/IP model?
What OSI layer does encryption (TLS) operate at, and why does that matter for security architecture?
anchors: Top-down mnemonic: "All People Seem To Need Data Processing" (7→1: Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical).
Bottom-up mnemonic: "Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away" (1→7).
PDU chain: Bits (1) → Frames (2) → Packets (3) → Segments (4) — memorize this order since it's a very common fill-in-the-blank interview question.
"Switches switch frames (Layer 2), routers route packets (Layer 3)" — a quick way to recall device-to- layer mapping.
sessions.summary: The OSI model, what each layer actually does, and where real devices sit.

sessions.title: TCPIPModel

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: How many layers does the TCP/IP model have, and how do they map onto the seven OSI layers?
Why does the industry use TCP/IP in practice instead of the full OSI protocol suite?
What's the difference between the Internet layer and the Transport layer, in terms of what each one is responsible for?
If a firewall rule blocks a connection, which TCP/IP layer(s) does that rule typically operate at, and what fields does it match on?
Explain the difference between checking IP-layer reachability (ping) and Transport-layer reachability (port test) — why might one succeed while the other fails?
anchors: "OSI has 7 seats, TCP/IP has 4 — and 3 of OSI's seats (App/Pres/Session) got merged into TCP/IP's one Application seat, while OSI's bottom 2 (Data Link/Physical) got merged into TCP/IP's one Network Access seat."
Four-layer order, top to bottom: Application, Transport, Internet, Network Access — "A Tiny Internet Network."
Layer-to-question mapping: Internet layer answers "can I reach the IP?"; Transport layer answers "can I reach the port?"; Application layer answers "does the service actually respond correctly?"
TCP/IP is the model of what's actually deployed; OSI is the model of how we talk about it.
sessions.summary: The TCP/IP model and how it maps onto OSI. Encapsulation and headers.

sessions.title: Ethernet

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is a MAC address, how is it structured, and how is it different from an IP address?

sessions.title: Routing Protocols

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is the fundamental difference between a distance-vector and a link-state routing protocol?
Two routes to the same prefix are learned via OSPF and EIGRP. Which one is installed, and why?

anchors: OSPF = a cartographer. Every router draws the exact same complete map (LSDB) and independently calculates the shortest route on it — nobody has to trust anyone else's opinion, they trust the map.

EIGRP = a driver with a pre-planned detour already memorized. If the main road closes, they don't stop to ask for directions (query neighbors) — they already know a guaranteed-safe backup route (Feasible Successor) and take it instantly.

BGP = an immigration checkpoint. Every route carries a stamped passport (AS-Path) showing every country (Autonomous System) it passed through; a router rejects any route whose passport already has its own country stamped on it, which is exactly how it prevents loops.
Administrative Distance mnemonic: "Con-Stat-eB-EI-O-R-eE-iB" (0-1-20-90-110-120-170-200) — lower always wins, connected and static are always trusted over anything dynamic.

sessions.title: TCP

interview: What is the difference between flow control and congestion control in TCP?

anchors: Three-way handshake: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK — "I want to talk / okay, and I want to talk too / okay, let's go."
Four-way teardown: FIN → ACK → FIN → ACK — each side says goodbye independently, unlike the handshake's combined SYN-ACK step.
Flow control = receiver's rulebook ("how much I can hold"); Congestion control = sender's rulebook ("how much the network can hold") — two separate windows, two separate purposes.
Fast retransmit trigger = 3 duplicate ACKs — remember "three strikes, resend."
SYN cookies defend against SYN floods by not committing memory until the handshake actually completes — "don't pay until they show up."

WPA2/3-Personal = one shared house key for everyone. WPA2/3-Enterprise = individual key cards issued and revocable per person (802.1X/RADIUS).
Sticky client = a phone call you refuse to hang up even though you've walked into the next room and can barely hear anymore — 802.11k/v/r exist to make you hang up and redial sooner.
sessions.summary: Wireless: channels, interference, and how 802.11 differs from Ethernet.

sessions.title: Directory Services

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is a directory service, and how is it different from a general relational database?
What is a Distinguished Name, and why does it matter?
Why do enterprise directory services use replication, and what's the difference between single- master and multi-master replication?
Why is a directory service considered a particularly high-value target for attackers?
A new employee's account works for logging into their laptop but not for an internal web application. What would you check?
anchors: Directory service = the organization's single phone book and org chart combined, that every other system looks up instead of keeping its own.
DIT = a tree, just like a filesystem — OUs are folders, entries are files, and a Distinguished Name is the full file path.
X.500 = the ambitious, heavyweight original blueprint. LDAP = the practical, TCP/IP-friendly version everyone actually built on.
Replication = photocopies of the phone book kept at every office, all kept in sync, so no single office losing power stops everyone else from looking someone up.
The directory is the root of trust — compromise it, and you've potentially compromised everything that trusts it, not just one system.
sessions.summary: Directory services: what a directory is, and why nearly everything binds to one.

sessions.title: Active Directory

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is the difference between a domain, a tree, and a forest in Active Directory?
What are FSMO roles, and why does AD need them if replication is multi-master?
Why is DNS described as a hard requirement for Active Directory, rather than just a helpful dependency?
What's happening, and how would you approach it?
How does AD's use of Sites improve performance in a multi-office organization?
anchors: AD = Session 51's generic directory concept, plus Kerberos, plus DNS integration, plus Group Policy, all bundled into one deeply interconnected Microsoft platform.
Domain Controller = a Windows Server holding a copy of NTDS.dit and answering "who is this, and what do they belong to" for its domain.

FSMO roles = the handful of jobs AD refuses to multi-master, because two DCs doing them simultaneously would cause chaos — think of them as five specific "single-signature-required" duties in an otherwise fully collaborative team.
Sites = AD's awareness of physical geography, so a laptop in the branch office doesn't waste 30 seconds authenticating across a WAN link to the head office.
SID, not name, is the real identity — renaming is safe, deleting-and-recreating is not.
sessions.summary: Active Directory: the forest, domain, DC and Global Catalog, and how a client finds them.

sessions.title: LDAP

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What's the difference between LDAP and Active Directory?
Why is StartTLS generally preferred over LDAPS?
What does an LDAP result code 49 mean?
What's an LDAP injection attack?
anchors: DN reads like a mailing address, most specific first: 'cn (person), ou (department), dc (company)' — the reverse of how you'd write a street address, but the same idea of nesting.
389 is plain, 636 is a lock (6-3-6 — three extra digits, like a padlock combination, to remember it's the 'secured' one).
Bind = login. Search = look something up. Everything else (Add/Modify/Delete/ModifyDN) is 'the four ways to change the tree.'
'Search then bind' — the two-step pattern for username-based login: first find the DN, then authenticate as that DN.
sessions.summary: LDAP: the protocol under AD, bind types, and how to query it.

sessions.title: Kerberos

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: Why does Windows prefer Kerberos over NTLM?
What is a Golden Ticket attack?
A user reports Kerberos authentication failures that started this morning. What's the first thing you check?
What's the difference between a TGT and a service ticket?
anchors: Three-headed dog, three parties: client, service, and the trusted KDC standing between them — the mythology maps directly onto the protocol's actual shape.
'TGT unlocks the ticket window; the service ticket unlocks the door.' Two different tickets, two different purposes — don't present a TGT directly to an application.
Port 88 for Kerberos — small number, first thing that happens at 'logon time.'
Clock skew breaks Kerberos before passwords ever do — when in doubt, check NTP first.
sessions.summary: Kerberos: tickets, the KDC, and why time skew breaks authentication.

sessions.title: NTLM

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What's the main structural difference between NTLM and Kerberos authentication?
What is pass-the-hash, and why does it work against NTLM?
Why would a domain-joined machine fall back to NTLM even though Kerberos is fully configured?
How would you reduce NTLM usage in an environment without breaking things?
anchors: Three messages: Negotiate → Challenge → Authenticate — 'N-C-A,' the opposite order of Kerberos' 'you prove yourself first' flow; here the server challenges you first.
'The hash IS the key' — unlike a password, if an attacker has the NT hash, they don't need to crack it to use it. That's the whole pass-the-hash problem in one line.
Member servers can't validate NTLM alone — they have to phone a Domain Controller (Netlogon) every time. Kerberos services validate locally. That's the structural cost of NTLM's design.
IP address instead of hostname = no SPN = no Kerberos = NTLM fallback, guaranteed.
sessions.summary: NTLM: the older protocol, its weaknesses, and how it still appears in mixed networks.

sessions.title: DNS Integration AD

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: Why does Active Directory depend so heavily on DNS?
What is the _msdcs zone/subdomain and why is it significant?
A remote office's workstations are logging in successfully but slowly. What would you check first?
What's the security risk of allowing unrestricted dynamic DNS updates?
anchors: 'DC Locator runs before Kerberos, before LDAP, before anything else' — DNS is the very first hop in any domain logon, which is why it's the first thing worth checking, not the last.
SRV record = 'where's the service,' not 'what's the IP' — a fundamentally different question than an A record answers.
_msdcs = forest-wide, site-scoped SRV = site-local preference — two layers of the same discovery mechanism, one broad, one local.
'AD-integrated' means the DNS data lives inside AD's own database, replicated by AD itself — not a separate system that merely talks to AD.
sessions.summary: How AD DNS actually works: SRV records, the _msdcs zones, and why DNS breaks join first.

sessions.title: Trusts

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: If Domain A trusts Domain B, who can access what?
What's the difference between a trust and simply granting file permissions to a user?
What is SID filtering and why does it matter for forest trusts?
What's a Shortcut Trust and when would you use one?
anchors: 'The trusting domain opens its door; the trusted domain's users are the ones who get to walk through it.' Trust direction = direction of access being granted, always.
Trust answers 'can I believe you,' permissions answer 'are you allowed in' — two separate questions, both required.
Transitive = 'flows downstream automatically' (A trusts B trusts C, so A trusts C); non-transitive = 'stops exactly where you drew the line.'
Referral tickets are Kerberos's way of saying 'I don't handle this realm, but I know someone who does' — the cross-realm equivalent of a phone transfer to the right department.
sessions.summary: Trusts: one-way, two-way, transitive, and the security cost of each.

sessions.title: Forests

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is Active Directory's actual security boundary — the domain or the forest?
What is the Global Catalog and why does it exist?
When would an organization choose a multi-domain forest over a single-domain forest?
Why might a security team deploy a separate, dedicated forest just for privileged administrative accounts?
anchors: 'Forest = the whole property, Domain = a building on it.' Different buildings can have different local rules (password policy), but the property line (schema, forest-wide trust, Enterprise Admins) is shared by everyone on the lot.
Global Catalog = 'the whole forest's yellow pages, abridged' — full detail for your own domain, quick-reference summary for everyone else's.
3268/3269 = Global Catalog ports, always paired mentally with 389/636 from Session 53 as 'the forest-wide version of the same idea.'
If it says 'Enterprise Admins' or 'Schema Admins,' think forest-wide, not domain-wide — a completely different blast radius than 'Domain Admins.'
sessions.summary: Forests, domains and the Global Catalog as the price of scale.

sessions.title: Domains

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: Strong Answer What's the difference between a domain, a tree, and a forest?
Why can a compromised workstation credential still lead to full domain compromise?
What are the three domain-level FSMO roles and what does each do?
Why would an organization choose multiple domains over one domain with OUs?
How does a Golden Ticket attack work, and what does it target?
anchors: Domain = the smallest security boundary with its own database partition, password policy, and admin group — think "the actual walls," where a forest is "the property line."
Three domain-only FSMO roles: RID (IDs), PDC Emulator (time + legacy + urgent changes), Infrastructure (cross-domain references) — remember as "IDs, Time, References."
Every domain login is DNS → Kerberos → Database: find the DC, prove who you are, look up what you're allowed to do.
Domain Admins group = keys to the kingdom; Tier 0 protection exists specifically because of this.
Entra ID is a cousin, not a clone — flat tenant, web protocols, synced from on-prem via Entra Connect in most real deployments.
sessions.summary: Domains, OUs, and structuring an object model that survives staff turnover.

sessions.title: Group Policy

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: Strong Answer What order does Group Policy apply in, and which setting wins on conflict?
What's the difference between Enforced and Block Inheritance, and which wins if both are used?
Why can Group Policy changes take a while to show up on a machine?
What's stored in the GPC vs. the GPT, and why does that split matter?
How would you find out why a specific setting isn't applying to a specific machine?
anchors: LSDOU — Local, Site, Domain, OU — the processing order, closest-to-object wins by default.
Enforced beats Block Inheritance — the one exception that flips normal precedence, and a favorite interview trap.
GPC in AD (metadata) + GPT in SYSVOL (actual files) — two storage locations, two replication paths, one common source of "it's inconsistent" bugs.
90 minutes + random offset = the default refresh cycle; gpupdate /force to skip the wait.
gpresult /h report.html — the one command that turns "why isn't this applying" from a guess into a five-minute answer.
sessions.summary: Group Policy: scopes, security filtering, and the order settings apply in.

sessions.title: PKI

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: Strong Answer What's the difference between the public key and the private key, and which one is ever shared?

Why is the root CA typically kept offline? Because its private key is the ultimate trust anchor for every certificate ever issued beneath it; if compromised, the entire chain of trust it built collapses, so exposure is minimized by only powering it on to sign new intermediates.
What's the difference between CRL and OCSP, and what problem does OCSP stapling solve?
A user's browser shows 'certificate not trusted' for an internal site — what do you check first?
Why might an organization use a private CA Public devices (customers' browsers) only trust publicly- Question Strong Answer for internal services but a public CA for its customer-facing website?
anchors: Public key shared, private key secret, signature proves possession of the private key without revealing it.
Root offline, intermediate online — protect the trust anchor by minimizing its exposure.
CRL = list you download; OCSP = question you ask live; stapling = the server asks so the client doesn't have to.
A certificate is a signed statement: "this public key belongs to this identity," nothing more.
Internal PKI needs its root pushed to trust stores (via Group Policy); public PKI is already trusted everywhere by default.
sessions.summary: PKI: what a certificate authority is for and how trust anchors work.

sessions.title: Certificates

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: Strong Answer Why does a certificate with the correct Subject field sometimes still fail hostname validation?
What's the practical difference between Key Usage and Extended Key Usage?
What's the difference between PEM, DER, and PKCS#12, and when would you use each?
What's the security trade-off of using a wildcard certificate versus individual or SAN certificates?
Strong Answer A browser reports 'unable to verify the first certificate' — what's the most likely cause and how would you confirm it?
anchors: SAN, not Subject CN, is what hostname validation actually checks today.
Key Usage = what the key can cryptographically do; EKU = what purpose it's allowed to serve — both can silently block an otherwise-valid certificate.
PEM is text, DER is binary, PKCS#12 (.pfx) bundles cert+key+chain together with a password.
Wildcard = convenience with concentrated blast radius; SAN/per-service certs = more management overhead, smaller blast radius.
openssl x509 -text -noout is the go-to command to actually read what's inside a certificate rather than guessing.
sessions.summary: Certificates: issuing, renewal, and the expiry outage nobody planned for.

sessions.title: Federation ADFS

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: Strong Answer What problem does federation solve that a domain trust (Session 59) doesn't?
What is a Golden SAML attack, and why is it dangerous?
Why might seamless SSO fail for a user working from home but succeed in the office?
What's the practical difference between SAML and OIDC that would influence which to use for a new integration?
anchors: IdP issues and signs, SP trusts and consumes — the password never crosses that boundary.
SAML = XML, older, enterprise-classic; OIDC = JWT, newer, built on OAuth 2.0.
Golden SAML is Golden Ticket's federation-layer cousin — steal the signing key, forge trust for anyone, anywhere it's trusted.
Seamless SSO = the same Kerberos TGT from Session 59 doing double duty at the federation layer.
Claim Rules decide what gets asserted; a misconfigured rule is an over-privileging risk, not just a broken-login risk.
sessions.summary: Federation and ADFS: joining two identity worlds without duplicating passwords.

sessions.title: SSO

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is the difference between SAML and OIDC, and when would you choose one over the other?
What does an SP actually validate when it receives a SAML assertion or an OIDC ID token? What happens if it skips signature validation?
Why does SSO require accurate time synchronization between the IdP and SP?
How does Kerberos-based Integrated Windows Authentication differ from SAML/OIDC-based SSO?
What is the difference between SSO (authentication) and SCIM (provisioning), and why do enterprises need both?
If a user reports they can log into the IdP fine but get 'access denied' inside the application, what would you check first?
anchors: SSO = one login, many doors — the IdP hands the user a signed 'note' the SP trusts instead of asking for a password itself.
SAML = XML wearing a suit to a 2005 enterprise meeting. OIDC = JSON built for phones and APIs.
The SP never touches the password — think 'bouncer checks the wristband, doesn't ask who put it on.'
Golden SAML = someone steals the stamp the bouncer uses to make wristbands, so they can make their own.
Kerberos SSO on the intranet = the ticket you got at the front gate this morning gets silently re- shown at every door inside — no new asking.
sessions.summary: Single sign-on: the promise, the trade-offs, and where it breaks.

sessions.title: MFA

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What makes something a valid 'second factor' — why doesn't a password plus a security question count as MFA?
Why is SMS considered the weakest common MFA method? What specific attack defeats it?
What is MFA fatigue / push bombing, and what control specifically mitigates it?
How does step-up or risk-based authentication differ from requiring MFA on every single login?
If a user reports their SSH MFA prompt never appears, what would you check first on the Linux server?
Why can legacy authentication protocols like IMAP/POP3 undermine an otherwise strong MFA policy?
anchors: MFA = know + have + are — mix categories, not copies. Two passwords is not MFA, it's just one factor said twice.
TOTP = a stopwatch both sides share — no network call needed because the code is 'time plus secret,' computed independently on both ends.
SMS MFA is a screen door — better than nothing, but SIM swapping walks right through it.
AiTM phishing beats TOTP/push because it just relays what you typed/approved in real time — but it can't relay a FIDO2 signature, because that signature is glued to the real website's address.
Push bombing = knocking until someone answers by accident — number-matching stops the 'accidental yes.'
sessions.summary: Multi-factor authentication: factors, fatigue attacks, and recovery paths.

sessions.title: Identity Governance

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is the Joiner-Mover-Leaver model, and why is the 'Mover' event often the weakest link in practice?
Why does RBAC make access certification more tractable than reviewing individual permissions directly?
What is 'privilege creep' and what specific governance control is designed to counteract it?
How does Identity Governance differ from what SSO and MFA already provide?
What does 'rubber-stamp' certification mean, and how would you detect it happening in a review campaign?
Why is same-day leaver deprovisioning treated as a higher-priority automation than the quarterly certification cycle?
How would you reconcile a case where Active Directory group membership doesn't match what the governance platform believes it granted?
anchors: Governance answers 'should you still have this,' not 'are you who you say you are' — that's SSO/MFA's job.
Joiner-Mover-Leaver: grants pile up easily, but only a deliberate process takes them back down — like a closet that only gets cleaned on a schedule, not automatically.
RBAC = review the bundle, not every item — a manager certifies 'Finance Analyst,' not twenty separate permissions.
SoD = don't let one person write the check AND sign it — the classic fraud-prevention conflict rule.
Rubber-stamp certification is worse than no certification — it creates false assurance that something was checked when it wasn't.
sessions.summary: Identity governance: joiners, movers and leavers as a security control.

sessions.title: DNS Enterprise

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is the difference between AD-integrated DNS zones and traditional primary/secondary zone replication?
What is a dangling DNS record, and why does it create a subdomain takeover risk?
Why should zone transfers be restricted to specific IP addresses, and what mechanism authenticates a transfer?
How does dynamic DNS update security differ between an AD-integrated zone (GSS-TSIG) and a traditional BIND setup (TSIG)?
In a hybrid on-prem/cloud environment, how would you let each side resolve the other's private namespace without merging the zones?
anchors: DNS is the layer everything else silently trusts — when it breaks, the symptoms look like everything else's problem first.
Split-horizon = same question, different room, different answer — internal LAN vs internet gets a different IP for the same name.
A dangling CNAME is an unlocked door with your company's name still painted on it — decommission the resource, decommission the record, same pipeline.
AD-integrated DNS = many masters, one truth, replicated — no single primary bottleneck because AD's replication does the work.
DNSSEC signs, it doesn't hide — think 'tamper-evident seal,' not 'privacy envelope.'
sessions.summary: Enterprise DNS design: zones, delegation, forwarders and caching.

sessions.title: DHCP Enterprise Deployment

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: A user's laptop shows a 169.254.x.x address. What does that tell you, and what would you check first?
How would you design DHCP redundancy for a site with 500 users, with no tolerance for an outage during a single server failure?
What is DHCP snooping and what specific attack does it primarily defend against?
Why does Windows require DHCP servers to be authorized in Active Directory, and what problem does that solve?
A whole VLAN suddenly gets the wrong default gateway. What's your triage process?
How does DHCP interact with DNS in an Active Directory environment (DDNS)? What could go wrong with that integration?
anchors: DORA = Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge — the same four steps from Session 40, now happening across scopes, relays, and redundant servers instead of one flat network.
T1 = 50% (quiet renewal), T2 = 87.5% (broadcast rebind), 100% = full restart from Discover — the '50 / 87.5 / 100' progression is the whole lease lifecycle in three numbers.
APIPA (169.254.x.x) on a screen = the device's own admission that DHCP completely failed — it's the network equivalent of a blank stare.
“Untrusted ports drop Offers” is the one-line summary of DHCP snooping.
sessions.summary: Deploying DHCP at enterprise scale: scopes, reservations, failover and relay.

sessions.title: NTP

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: Why does Kerberos care about clock synchronization, and what's the default tolerance?
Why does NTP prefer slewing the clock over stepping it, and when would it step instead?
In an Active Directory forest, which server is the authoritative internal time source by default, and how does that get configured?
A user reports a certificate error on an internal site that was working yesterday. How does clock drift factor into your troubleshooting?
What is an NTP amplification attack, and how do you prevent your NTP infrastructure from being used in one?
How would you propagate correct time to a network switch or appliance that isn't a domain member?
anchors: Stratum 0 = the atomic/GPS clock itself (not on the network); Stratum 1 = directly attached to it;
every layer after that is one hop further from the truth.
“Five minutes” is the Kerberos magic number — the single most common real-world reason NTP suddenly matters to someone who's never thought about it before.
PDC Emulator = the one domain controller role responsible for being the forest's authoritative internal clock, by default.
Slew, don't step — NTP prefers gently nudging the clock over jumping it, protecting anything mid- flight (auth tickets, running processes) from a sudden time jump.
sessions.summary: Time synchronisation: NTP/chrony, and why unsynchronised clocks cause outages.

sessions.title: File Servers

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: Explain how NTFS permissions and share permissions interact when a user accesses a folder over the network. Which one wins?
Why is it considered best practice to leave share permissions permissive and do granular control at the NTFS level?
What is DFS Namespaces, and what problem does it solve that a plain file share doesn't?
A user says a file they need is missing. What's your triage process before escalating to a full backup restore?
Why should permissions be assigned to AD security groups rather than individual users directly?
How would you detect and respond to a ransomware event affecting a shared file server?
What's the difference between a Shadow Copy and a backup, and when would you use each for file recovery?
How would you design an onboarding process so a new employee automatically gets correct file share access on day one?
anchors: “Most restrictive wins” — the one sentence that explains every confusing NTFS-vs-share permission ticket you'll ever troubleshoot.
Groups, not people — permissions go on AD security groups; people go in the groups. Never the other way around.
DFS = the 'one path, many possible servers behind it' trick — users never need to know which physical server they're actually talking to.
Shadow Copy = self-service time machine for one file; Backup = the real safety net for the whole server.
sessions.summary: File services: shares, permissions, quotas, and the NTFS vs share distinction.

sessions.title: Print Servers

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: A print queue is completely stuck. What's your troubleshooting order of operations?
What is Point and Print, and what security risk does it introduce?
What was PrintNightmare, at a conceptual level, and why is it a good example of a 'boring service, serious risk' vulnerability?
Why would an enterprise disable the print spooler service on its domain controllers specifically?
What is printer pooling and when would you use it?
How would you deploy a new shared printer to exactly the right group of users without manual per-machine setup?
What's the difference between direct IP printing and using a central print server, and what do you lose by skipping the server?
anchors: Jobs print in strict order — one bad job at the top blocks every good job behind it. Check the top of the queue first, always.
Spooler = the queue engine; Driver = the translator; Port = where the job actually goes. A failure in any one looks like 'printing is broken' but needs a different fix.
PrintNightmare = the permanent reminder that 'just a print service' can mean SYSTEM-level compromise.
Point and Print = convenient auto-driver install for users, and exactly the same mechanism an attacker would want to abuse if the server weren't trusted.
sessions.summary: Print services: queues, drivers, and why printing breaks on every migration.

sessions.title: Application Servers

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What's the difference between a web server and an application server, and where's the boundary in a typical request?
How would you handle session state in a horizontally scaled application server cluster?
What's the difference between container-managed and programmatic transaction management?
A node in your app server cluster is unhealthy but the load balancer hasn't removed it yet — what could cause that, and how would you fix the health-check config?
Why is thread-per-request less memory-efficient than an event-loop model, and when would you still choose it?
How do you securely handle database credentials for an application server without hardcoding them?
anchors: Think of the three-tier model as a restaurant: the web tier is the waiter (takes orders, delivers food, doesn't cook), the application server is the kitchen (executes the actual work, manages multiple orders in flight, has a fixed number of stoves = connection pool), and the database is the pantry (source of truth for ingredients/state).
Connection pool exhaustion = too many chefs trying to grab too few stoves — everyone queues, service slows, and orders start timing out even though the kitchen 'looks' fine from the outside.

Sticky session vs. externalized session = "the waiter always seats you at the same table" vs. "your order ticket is in a shared system any waiter can pull up" — the second survives a waiter calling in sick.
sessions.summary: Application servers: deployment, runtime, and service management.

sessions.title: Database Servers

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: How does a Write-Ahead Log enable crash recovery, and what's the difference between redo and undo?
What's the tradeoff between synchronous and asynchronous replication, and which would you choose for a financial ledger vs. an analytics replica?
Why can adding an index make writes slower even though it speeds up reads?
When would you choose a NoSQL database over a relational database, and what do you give up?
How would you diagnose replication lag between a primary and a read replica?
What's the difference between pessimistic locking and MVCC, and why might a database prefer MVCC for read-heavy workloads?
anchors: Think of the Write-Ahead Log as a ship's logbook: the captain writes "course changed to 090" in the log before actually turning the wheel, so if the ship loses power mid-turn, anyone reading the log afterward knows exactly what should have happened and can finish the turn.

ACID's Isolation property is like people editing the same shared spreadsheet: full isolation (Serializable) is like passing the spreadsheet one person at a time — safest but slowest; low isolation is like everyone editing simultaneously and occasionally seeing each other's half-finished edits — fast but riskier.
Replication lag is a photocopier that's a few pages behind the original document being written — ask it for page 50 while it's still on page 47, and you get stale information, not an error.
sessions.summary: Database servers: installing, initialising and securing a database service.

sessions.title: Web Servers

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What's the difference between a web server and an application server, in your own words?
How does HTTP/2 multiplexing improve on HTTP/1.1 keep-alive, and what limitation does it still not solve?
You're seeing 502 errors from your web tier — what's your triage process?
How would you diagnose a Slowloris-style denial-of-service attack, and how would you mitigate it?
What's the tradeoff between Apache's process-per-connection model and Nginx's event-driven model?
Where should TLS be terminated in a typical enterprise architecture, and why?
How does a CDN change the role and load profile of your origin web server?
anchors: Think of the web server as a hotel front desk: it can hand you your room key directly for something simple (static content) or, for anything more complex, pick up the phone and route your request to the right department (the application server) without you ever needing to know that department's internal extension.

Worker connection exhaustion is the front desk running out of staff during a rush — the hotel isn't out of rooms (the app servers are fine), it just can't process check-ins fast enough to get guests to those rooms.
HTTP/2 multiplexing is like one phone line carrying several interleaved conversations at once instead of hanging up and redialing for every single sentence, the way HTTP/1.1 without keep-alive would.
sessions.summary: Web servers: Apache httpd, virtual hosts, TLS termination.

sessions.title: Reverse Proxy

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What's the difference between a forward proxy and a reverse proxy?
Why does a reverse proxy need to overwrite, not append to, the X-Forwarded-For header?
What is HTTP request smuggling, and how does it relate to how a proxy and backend parse request framing?
How is a reverse proxy different from a load balancer, and how is an API gateway different from both?
How would you implement a canary release using reverse proxy routing rules?
Why might a reverse proxy be a single point of failure, and how do you mitigate that?
anchors: Think of a reverse proxy as a corporate receptionist: visitors (clients) only ever interact with the receptionist, who decides which internal office (backend) to send them to, and the internal org chart can be reshuffled endlessly without visitors ever needing new directions.

X-Forwarded-For is like a delivery driver handing off a package to a second driver at a relay point — the label needs to say who the original sender was, or the final recipient has no way to know, since all they see is the second driver's face.

Overlapping routing rules are like two receptionists both listening for the phrase "I'm here for the finance department" — whichever one answers first wins, regardless of which one was technically the better match.
sessions.summary: Reverse proxies: TLS offload, header rewriting, and health checks.

sessions.title: Proxy

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What's the difference between a forward proxy and a reverse proxy, in terms of who it represents?
How does SSL/TLS inspection work, and what real risks does deploying it introduce?
What's the difference between explicit and transparent proxying, and what are the tradeoffs of each?
A business-critical app breaks only when SSL inspection is enabled — what's your troubleshooting approach?
Why would an enterprise choose a cloud-delivered Secure Web Gateway over an on-prem proxy appliance?
How does an open proxy misconfiguration become a security risk to parties outside your organization?
How would you design logging and authentication on a forward proxy to support an incident investigation after the fact?
anchors: Think of a forward proxy as a corporate mailroom: every outgoing package (request) from every employee passes through the mailroom first, which can inspect, log, or refuse to send certain packages according to company policy, and the outside world only ever sees the mailroom's return address, never the individual employee's desk.

SSL inspection is the mailroom opening a sealed envelope, reading it, resealing it in a new envelope with the mailroom's own seal, and sending it onward — which only works because everyone inside the building has agreed in advance to trust the mailroom's seal (the internal CA certificate).

Certificate pinning breaking through SSL inspection is like a recipient who was told "only accept mail sealed with the original sender's exact seal" — a resealed envelope, even from a trusted mailroom, gets rejected on sight.
sessions.summary: Forward proxies: filtering, caching, and egress control.

sessions.title: Storage SAN NAS
interview: What is the fundamental difference between SAN and NAS, and how does that difference affect which use cases each is suited for?
Explain LUN masking and zoning — why are both needed instead of just one?
Compare Fibre Channel and iSCSI. When would you choose one over the other?
Why does RAID 6 exist when RAID 5 already tolerates a disk failure?
How does MPIO improve storage resilience, and what happens if it's misconfigured?
How would you troubleshoot a virtualization host that suddenly cannot see one of its datastores?
What is the cloud equivalent of a SAN LUN, and how does that mapping help you reason about cloud architectures?
anchors: SAN = block, like handing someone a stack of blank ledger pages — they decide how to rule and organize them. NAS = file, like handing someone a fully organized, labeled filing cabinet — the organization is already done for them.
Zoning is the fabric's guest list (who's allowed at the party); LUN masking is the individual room assignment once inside (which room each guest may enter).
RAID 5 = one spare tire; RAID 6 = two spare tires — useful when a rebuild after the first flat takes long enough that a second flat becomes a real risk.

17. Connections — Ties to Prior Sessions Storage sits directly downstream of the physical hardware layer (Sessions 1–9): disks, controllers, and power redundancy inside every array are the same fundamentals studied there, just at enterprise density and scale.

It depends on the networking layer (Sessions 25–50) for its transport — Ethernet switching and VLANs for iSCSI/NAS traffic, subnetting and routing for reachability, and ACLs for isolating storage traffic from general user traffic.
sessions.summary: Storage: SAN vs NAS, iSCSI, NFS, and the trade-offs.

sessions.title: Backup
interview: What is the difference between an incremental and a differential backup, and how does that affect restore time?
Why is a snapshot on the same array not considered a true backup?
What does 'application-consistent' backup mean, and why does it matter for databases?
How do immutable backups protect against ransomware specifically, compared to regular backups?
How would you validate that your backups are actually usable, not just present?
anchors: 3-2-1 is a fire drill in numbers: 3 copies so no single loss is fatal, 2 media types so no single defect kills both, 1 off-site so no single building can take everything with it.
A snapshot is a bookmark in the same book — useful, but burn the book and the bookmark is gone too. A backup is a photocopy kept in a different building.

Incremental backups are like saving only 'today's diff' — fast to write, but you need every page since the last full chapter to reconstruct the story. Differential backups are like re-summarizing everything since the last full chapter in one go — slower to write, faster to reconstruct.

17. Connections — Ties to Prior Sessions Backup builds directly on enterprise storage (Session 77): the same SAN/NAS systems that host production data are also frequently the snapshot source, and dedicated backup targets follow the same RAID/erasure-coding and networking principles introduced there.

It depends on the identity layer (Session 52, Active Directory) for service account permissions, on NTP (Session 69) for scheduling and retention accuracy, and on networking (Sessions 27–33, 43–44) for moving potentially large data volumes to off-site or cloud targets within backup windows.
sessions.summary: Backup: full, incremental and differential, and why backup is not restore.

sessions.title: High Availability
interview: What is the difference between High Availability, fault tolerance, and disaster recovery?
Compare active/active and active/passive HA architectures — what are the tradeoffs?
What is a Virtual IP, and how does it enable transparent failover?
Why is 'five nines' availability so much harder to achieve than 'three nines'?
Why does HA for a database require more than just compute-layer redundancy?
How would you safely test that a production HA cluster's failover actually works?
anchors: Quorum is a jury, not a single witness: a majority must agree a node is really gone before anyone is allowed to act as if it is — this is exactly what prevents split-brain.
A Virtual IP is a name tag passed between understudies: the audience (client) never needs to know which understudy is currently wearing it, only that the show (service) keeps going.

HA vs. Backup vs. DR is a three-part safety net: HA catches a single component falling (seconds), Backup catches data being ruined (restore from a point in time), DR catches the whole building falling (site-level recovery).

17. Connections — Ties to Prior Sessions High Availability builds directly on enterprise storage (Session 77), which supplies the shared or replicated data layer that makes failover meaningful rather than just moving compute to a node with no current data. It also builds on Backup (Session 78), which remains necessary for the class of failures — deletion, corruption, ransomware — that HA by design does not address.

It depends on network-layer redundancy protocols (STP, LACP — Sessions 34–35) and load balancing (Session 48) for both the failover network path and active/active traffic distribution, and on DNS (Session 39/67) for name resolution and some failover mechanisms.
sessions.summary: High availability: failover clustering, load balancing, and quorum.

sessions.title: Disaster Recovery
interview: What is the difference between RTO and RPO, and how do they drive DR architecture decisions?
Compare cold, warm, and hot DR site strategies — what determines which one an organization should choose?
Why is synchronous replication usually limited to short distances, while asynchronous replication can span continents?
What is a tiered recovery strategy, and why don't all systems get the same RTO/RPO?
Why can replicating from a compromised production system during a cyberattack actually spread the compromise to the DR site?
How does Disaster Recovery differ from High Availability, and why do enterprises need both?
anchors: RTO answers 'how long until we're back,' RPO answers 'how much did we lose.' Think of RTO as the clock on the wall and RPO as the rewind point on the recording.
Cold, warm, hot DR sites are like a cold car engine, an idling engine, and a car already moving alongside you — each faster to use, each more expensive to keep ready.
HA catches you falling off a bike; DR is what happens when the whole bike shop burns down and you need a different shop entirely.

17. Connections — Ties to Prior Sessions Disaster Recovery is the capstone of the resilience trio introduced across Sessions 78–80: Backup (Session 78) provides the data, High Availability (Session 79) handles component-level failures, and DR formalizes the response when an event exceeds what either of those can absorb — an entire site or region becoming unavailable.

It depends on enterprise storage (Session 77) and networking (Sessions 29, 45–46) for replication between sites, on DNS (Session 39/67) for redirecting traffic during failover, and on identity services (Session 52) being restorable early in the recovery sequence so everything built on top of it can follow.
sessions.summary: Disaster recovery: RPO, RTO, and designing for the day it all fails.

sessions.title: Monitoring

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is the difference between monitoring and observability?
Why is p99 latency more useful than average latency for understanding user experience?
What is the difference between a counter, a gauge, and a histogram?
How would you design an alert to avoid both alert fatigue and missed incidents?
What is the difference between synthetic monitoring and real-user monitoring, and when would you use each?
Why does monitoring depend on accurate time synchronization (NTP)?
How would you monitor a system you don't have visibility into the code for?
How should alerting differ between a symptom-based alert and a cause-based alert?
anchors: Golden Signals = Latency, Traffic, Errors, Saturation — think "L-T-E-S," the four vital signs of any service.
Counter only goes up (like an odometer); Gauge goes up and down (like a fuel gauge); Histogram tells you the shape of the crowd, not just the average person in it.
Monitoring detects, Logging explains, Tracing locates — three different questions: "is something wrong," "what happened," "where in the request did it happen."
Synthetic monitoring is a robot user checking on a schedule; Real User Monitoring is measuring actual humans as they use the system.
If you can't silence an alert without it being logged, you don't actually have monitoring security — you have a false sense of it.
sessions.summary: Monitoring: what to watch, alert thresholds, and alert fatigue.

sessions.title: Logging

sections.label: Where it sits in the enterprise

interview: What is the difference between monitoring and logging, and why do you need both?
What is a correlation ID, and why is it necessary in a distributed system?
Why does log analysis depend so heavily on accurate time synchronization?
How would you design a log retention policy that balances cost, compliance, and investigative usefulness?
What is the difference between structured and unstructured logging, and why does it matter at scale?
How do you keep logs both useful for investigation and safe from an integrity/tampering standpoint?
What sensitive data should never appear in a log line, and how would you prevent it from leaking in?
